text: Was there an actual fire in the pantry or hall?
Did something the person did in the pantry trigger the fire alarm?

Did the person use a toaster, causing something to burn and set off the alarm?

Did the person burn incense in the pantry, and did its smoke trigger the alarm?

Did the cigarette smoke activate a smoke detector in or near the pantry, which caused the fire alarm to ring?

The person went to the pantry specifically to smoke a cigarette. The cigarette smoke reached a smoke detector in or near the pantry, setting it off and causing the fire alarm to ring. There was no actual fire.
Did the person intentionally set off the fire alarm by smoking, rather than merely setting it off accidentally?

Did a non-cigarette source of smoke or vapor in the pantry also contribute to setting off the alarm?

The person went to the pantry to smoke a tobacco cigarette with a group of other people; at least three people were smoking there at the same time. Their cigarette smoke reached the functioning smoke detector and caused the fire alarm to ring, although there was no actual fire. Another person’s use of an electrical device also contributed to the alarm, but the specific device and action are not established by the clues.

Did the electrical device contribute by producing a smell or odor that helped trigger the fire alarm?

The person went to the pantry to smoke a tobacco cigarette together with at least two other people. Their combined cigarette smoke reached a functioning smoke detector and set off the fire alarm; there was no fire. Someone else also used an electrical device in a way that contributed to the alarm, but the available clues do not establish what the device was or exactly how it contributed.
